lesson.title: Exponentials
lesson.body:
Anchors: e = 2.718, e2 = 7.389, e3 = 20.09, e4 = 54.6, e5 = 148.4, and √e = e0.5 ≈ 1.649. Exponents add, so e3.5 = e3 × √e ≈ 20.09 × 1.65 ≈ 33.1, and negatives are reciprocals: e−2 = 1/7.389 ≈ 0.135.

Small x: ex ≈ 1 + x + x²/2 (add x³/6 once |x| passes ~0.15). e0.12 ≈ 1 + 0.12 + 0.0072 = 1.127. e−0.25 ≈ 1 − 0.25 + 0.03125 − 0.0026 = 0.779.

Anything else: en × ef. Split x into the nearest half-integer plus a small remainder f (|f| ≤ 0.25), then multiply.

Example: e2.3 = e2.5 × e−0.2. e2.5 = 7.389 × 1.649 ≈ 12.18; e−0.2 ≈ 1 − 0.2 + 0.02 = 0.82 → 12.18 × 0.82 ≈ 9.99 (true 9.97).

Alternative: ex = 100.434x — convert, then use your powers-of-ten skill. Also handy: e0.693 = 2, e1.099 = 3, e2.303 = 10.

lesson.title: Powers
lesson.body:
Integer powers — break into pieces you know.

  • Change the base: 85 = 215 = 32 768; 57 = 107/27 = 78 125.
  • Square the half power: 74 = 492 = 2 401; 36 = 272 = 729.
  • Squares near a round number: a2 = (a − d)(a + d) + d2: 472 = 50 × 44 + 9 = 2 209.
  • Decimals: do the digits, then place the point: 1.13 → 1 331 → 1.331.

Fractional exponents — root first, then power. ap/q = (q√a)p: 274/3 = 34 = 81; 160.75 = 23 = 8. Half-integers use √: 26.5 = 64 × 1.414 ≈ 90.5; 102.5 ≈ 316.

Arbitrary ab — go through logs. ab = 10b·log a.

Example: 3.72.4. log 3.7 ≈ 0.602 − 0.434 × 0.3/4 = 0.569; × 2.4 = 1.366. 100.366: log 2.4 = 0.380 is 0.014 higher → 2.4 × (1 − 0.014/0.434) ≈ 2.32 → 23.2 (true 23.1). Keep three decimals in the log: the multiplication by b magnifies its error.

lesson.title: Roots
lesson.body:
Square roots: √(n² + d) ≈ n + d/2n. Find the nearest square, divide the leftover by twice its root. √52 = √(49 + 3) ≈ 7 + 3/14 ≈ 7.21 (true 7.211). Going down works too: √60 = √(64 − 4) ≈ 8 − 4/16 = 7.75 (true 7.746). It's the tangent line of √x, so it always slightly overshoots.

Big or small numbers: pair the exponent first. Write x = M × 10even with M between 10 and 1000, then √x = √M × 10half.

  • √52 000 = √520 × 101; √520 ≈ 23 − 9/46 ≈ 22.8 → 228.
  • √0.003 = √30 × 10−2 ≈ 5.48 × 0.01 = 0.0548.

Cube roots: ∛(n³ + d) ≈ n + d/3n², grouping the exponent in threes. ∛70 = ∛(64 + 6) ≈ 4 + 6/48 = 4.125 (true 4.121); ∛0.07 = ∛70 × 10−1 ≈ 0.412.

Higher roots: use logs. n√x = 10(log x)/n. 4√50: log 50 = 1.699; ÷ 4 = 0.425 → 100.425: log 2.7 = 0.431, a hair above → ≈ 2.66 (true 2.659).

lesson.title: Growth & rule of 72
lesson.body:
Why 72? Growing r per period doubles when n · ln(1 + r) = ln 2 = 0.693. For small r, ln(1 + r) ≈ r, giving n ≈ 69.3/r% — but ln(1 + r) is a bit less than r, so the true number is a bit larger. 72 corrects for that around 8 %, and it divides nicely by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12. Best all-round: 69.3/r + 0.35.

  • 6 %: 72/6 = 12 periods (true 11.9). 1 %: 69.3 + 0.35 ≈ 69.7. 25 %: 2.77 + 0.35 = 3.12.

Growth factors: (1 + r)n = en·ln(1 + r), with ln(1 + r) ≈ r − r²/2 (+ r³/3 for long horizons). Then find ey from the ln anchors: ln 2 = 0.693, ln 3 = 1.099, ln 5 = 1.609, ln 10 = 2.303, e = e1.

Example: 1.0612. ln 1.06 ≈ 0.06 − 0.0018 = 0.0582; × 12 = 0.698 ≈ ln 2 + 0.005 → 2 × 1.005 ≈ 2.01 (true 2.012).

Decay: −ln(1 − q) ≈ q + q²/2, so half-life ≈ 69.3/q − 0.35 (10 %/period: ≈ 6.6).

Required rate: to grow F× in N years, the continuous rate is ln F / N; the annual rate is eg − 1 ≈ g + g²/2. Triple in 20 years: 1.099/20 = 0.055 → 5.65 %.
